findings.title: Until issue 6 adds the flag, expiry is FAILED plus ERROR only ties issue ordering into a decision
The user-facing hook-timeout contract changes meaning and name
Findings converge on the hard exit's trigger
findings.why_it_matters: Two critics reach the hard exit from opposite sides. The hard exit exists so that "the event loop's cancel-and-await and the interpreter's thread join cannot hold the process until the supervisor kills it". Finding 3 shows it cannot fire when the thing holding the process is a blocked loop, because the decision runs on that loop. Finding 7 shows it fires when nothing is holding the process, because its trigger is a record written possibly days earlier, not something observed at exit. Each finding proposes its own local fix: a loop-independent watchdog thread for Finding 3, an exit-time observation for Finding 7. Should the hard exit's trigger be re-evaluated as one question (what actually holds a hassette process at exit, and who can observe it), or should the two be handled one at a time? Re-evaluation includes asking whether either failure mode is worth handling at all, or is a limitation to document.
findings.recommended: B: Keep the hard exit's trigger and address Findings 3 and 7 individually.
findings.chosen: B: Keep the hard exit's trigger and address Findings 3 and 7 individually.

findings.title: D19 bundles the runtime entry deadline with the exit topology, and the table scores L as if it lost the entry deadline
findings.why_it_matters: The entry deadline bounds runtime instance stops. The exit topology covers the two stages, the foundation budget, the 45s total and the grace changes. The two are independent: the entry deadline's clock starts after the app-key lock is held and never references either exit stage (design.md:614-617). The table still scores L's runtime-stop row as "Unbounded; wedges app-key lock silently" (design.md:585). That is a property of having no entry deadline, not of a single exit ceiling. The Pick-L condition then makes L require accepting runtime-stop hangs (design.md:658-659). One half of O has no opposition, and it carries the contested half with it. The critic's premise needs one correction. It says the exit topology exists only for an optional, telemetry-only snapshot (`shutdown_snapshot_path` defaults to `None`, config/models.py:61; deleting the database loses "only telemetry history", database-telemetry.md:128). The foundation stage also guarantees the session finalize, which carries D14's fatal reason, and the database drain (design.md:609-613). Under L, a hung app hook uses up the single ceiling, and the root force-terminates the foundation services with it (design.md:584, L column).
findings.recommended: B: Keep D19 whole. Re-score L's runtime-stop row to show that L can carry the entry deadline too. State that the foundation stage protects the session finalize (D14's fatal reason) and the drain, not only the snapshot, and rewrite the Pick-L condition to name all three.
findings.chosen: B: Keep D19 whole. Re-score L's runtime-stop row to show that L can carry the entry deadline too. State that the foundation stage protects the session finalize (D14's fatal reason) and the drain, not only the snapshot, and rewrite the Pick-L condition to name all three.

findings.title: Every deadline and the hard exit run on the event loop, so a hook that blocks the loop defeats all of them
findings.why_it_matters: The stage deadlines, the entry deadline's force-terminate and the hard exit are all asyncio timers or tasks. D19 covers a hook that swallows cancellation (design.md:597-603). It never covers a hook that blocks the loop, such as a synchronous `requests.get` with no timeout or `time.sleep` inside `async def on_shutdown`. While the loop is blocked, no deadline fires, no force-terminate runs and no hard exit happens. SIGTERM is delivered through the loop (server.py:68), so hassette cannot react, and the supervisor SIGKILLs at the grace period. The shutdown snapshot and session finalize are lost. The Done-when item "exits with its decided exit code instead of waiting for the supervisor to kill it" (design.md:750-752) is false for this case. Hassette's blocking-I/O detector warns about such calls by default (block_io_guard.py:36), but it does not stop them.
findings.recommended: A: Document blocked-loop hooks as out of scope. The supervisor's kill is the backstop. The app lifecycle docs say shutdown hooks must not block the loop, next to "must let cancellation through". The Done-when item excludes a blocked loop.
findings.chosen: A: Document blocked-loop hooks as out of scope. The supervisor's kill is the backstop. The app lifecycle docs say shutdown hooks must not block the loop, next to "must let cancellation through". The Done-when item excludes a blocked loop.

findings.title: Runtime force-termination reuses `_force_terminal()`, which leaves a FAILED app's listeners and jobs live
findings.why_it_matters: When the entry deadline expires, the instance is force-terminated, marked FAILED and flagged needs-restart while the process keeps running (design.md:614-624). `_force_terminal()` says it does not run `on_shutdown()` hooks, "so bus subscriptions and scheduler jobs owned by force-terminated resources are not cleaned up ... an accepted gap because force-terminal is nearly always followed by process exit" (base.py:372-376). An app's listeners and jobs are removed only in its `Bus`'s and `Scheduler`'s own `on_shutdown` (bus.py:184-197 calls `remove_all_listeners()`; scheduler.py:184-186 calls `remove_all_jobs()`). Those run in the post-hook stage, after the user hooks (base.py:637-648). If the deadline expires during or before that stage, `_force_terminal()` recurses into those children without running their hooks (base.py:427-428). The registrations stay with `BusService` and `SchedulerService`, so a FAILED app keeps acting on the house until hassette restarts. D10 promises the opposite for a cancelled init ("framework teardown removes its listeners and jobs", design.md:322). D12 then refuses any replacement, so the zombie handlers are the only copy of that app still running.
findings.recommended: A: In the Entry deadline bullet and issue 6's scope, state that expiry removes the instance's bus listeners and scheduler jobs by owner as part of force-termination. Removal is a registry operation and runs no user hook. Issue 1 or 6 implements it.
findings.chosen: A: In the Entry deadline bullet and issue 6's scope, state that expiry removes the instance's bus listeners and scheduler jobs by owner as part of force-termination. Removal is a registry operation and runs no user hook. Issue 1 or 6 implements it.

findings.title: The snapshot sits before the executor join, so a slow snapshot uses up the foundation budget and triggers a spurious hard exit
findings.why_it_matters: D19 orders the foundation stage as session finalize, then the database drain and close, then the executor join, under a 20s budget that sums their caps (design.md:609-613, 581). It also calls the snapshot "unbounded work inside the foundation stage, outside its budget" (design.md:584). In the code, the snapshot runs in `DatabaseService.on_shutdown`'s `finally`, after the close, and that hook awaits the shielded copy (database_service.py:347-350, 366-374). So the copy finishes before the database service is done, and the executor join can only start after it. The snapshot is inside the budget in practice. A copy longer than the budget's slack (about 19s once the finalize and drain finish quickly) expires the foundation stage before the join. The executor's threads are never joined, and that triggers the hard exit with an ERROR (design.md:612-613, 629-631). Result: a spurious "foundation stage did not finish" ERROR and an `os._exit` on a slow disk where nothing was wrong. The hard exit waits for the in-flight snapshot, so the copy itself still completes.
findings.recommended: A: Pin the snapshot as the foundation stage's last step, after the executor join and outside its budget, in the Foundation stage bullet.
findings.chosen: A: Pin the snapshot as the foundation stage's last step, after the executor join and outside its budget, in the Foundation stage bullet.
findings.choice_reason: Asked whether a hung snapshot outside the budget could be killed by anything; chose A after learning nothing kills it today under either option.

findings.title: The fixed 15s snapshot allowance halves the add-on's current margin, and a kill mid-copy is silent
findings.why_it_matters: The add-on sets `timeout: 60`, commented as covering "hassette's 30 s shutdown budget plus the database snapshot ... slow on SD cards" (hassette-addon config.yaml:11-15). That gives the snapshot 30s after a full-length stop. D19 raises the total to 45s and sizes the allowance at a fixed 15s (design.md:637-648). The add-on's 60s still equals 45 + 15, so its snapshot margin after a full-length stop halves. The operating docs warn that raising the total past 30s "risks Supervisor stopping Hassette before the snapshot is written" (operating.md:70). The allowance is a constant, while the snapshot is a full online backup of a database capped at 500 MB by default (models.py:74). When the supervisor kills mid-copy, the previous snapshot survives because of the rename (database_snapshot.py:28-66), so nothing is corrupted. But no log line is written, because the outcome callback never runs. The temp copy stays until `remove_stale_temps` deletes it after an hour (database_snapshot.py:24-25,69-75).
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: after a stop that runs to its full total on slow storage, the supervisor can kill the snapshot mid-copy, which leaves the previous snapshot in place and logs nothing.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: after a stop that runs to its full total on slow storage, the supervisor can kill the snapshot mid-copy, which leaves the previous snapshot in place and logs nothing.

findings.title: The hard exit is triggered by a process-lifetime record, not by what is left at exit
findings.why_it_matters: The hard exit fires "when a stage or entry deadline force-terminated something during the process's life" (design.md:629-630). An entry-deadline expiry days earlier makes every later clean shutdown skip the interpreter's teardown and log an ERROR "naming what was left". That work may have finished long ago, so the ERROR can be stale. Exit stays 0 by decision, so nothing else flags it. The operational-resilience critic adds that this final ERROR is logged after the database closes, so it reaches stdout and the supervisor log only, never the database log table the UI reads. Two of that critic's claims don't hold. The entry-deadline expiry does log an ERROR when it fires (design.md:620-622). The hard exit already "flushes logs" (design.md:632).
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: after a runtime entry-deadline expiry, the process's next shutdown hard-exits even if the force-terminated work has since finished, and its ERROR (stdout only) may name finished work.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: after a runtime entry-deadline expiry, the process's next shutdown hard-exits even if the force-terminated work has since finished, and its ERROR (stdout only) may name finished work.

findings.title: A needs-restart instance is invisible to the liveness probe the supervisor acts on
findings.why_it_matters: D4 and D11 keep a stuck app from affecting the process, so the needs-restart flag shows in the API, CLI and UI only. The add-on's Watchdog and Docker health checks call `/api/health/live`, which stays green. An unattended install with an app dead until restart has no automatic recovery and no external alert. This meets the Posture's "visible as a status and one ERROR" and matches HA's config-entry peer. It is a stance, not an oversight. D19's entry-deadline expiry is a new way to set this flag (design.md:618-623).
findings.chosen: Side B: Keep the flag in the API, CLI and UI only
